retrospective.harder_than_needed: Reconciling two DIFFERENT id spaces that the four AC-ORDER-* wordings conflate at a glance — applicationRumorDispatcher's dedup keys on the DECRYPTED rumor's inner `.id` field, while welcomeSubscription's dedup keys on the OUTER raw kind-445 NostrEvent id — required tracing both files' actual code (not just the AC prose) before the test harness design would hold together. AC-ORDER-1's phrase 'a sender-mismatched rumor sharing the same rumor id' only resolves cleanly once you see that a real forger can share the INNER id while necessarily using a DIFFERENT outer raw-event id (they can't reproduce another signer's exact bytes) — the welcomeSubscription-layer test had to model both ids explicitly (distinct outer ids, shared inner rumor id) to be a faithful, non-trivial proof rather than an accidental tautology. [Round 1] A first mutation attempt for VQ-S4-016 (firing a bogus onApplicationMessage call from the replay loop's 'newState' branch) silently passed all 50 tests for the wrong reason: that branch is dead code in the AC-ORDER-3 test's own outcome scenario (the replayed 'losing' commit's outcome is scripted as skippedPastEpoch, never newState, so ingest() never yields a processed+newState result during replay here). Confirming a mutation's non-detection is a REAL tautology (vs. an unreachable-branch false alarm) required re-deriving which result kinds the test's own fake-group outcome map can actually produce at each ingest() call site before concluding anything about test quality.
retrospective.surprised_by: epochResolver.ts's rollbackAndReplay re-emits an already-delivered application message through ingest() a SECOND time on every rollback (by design — the message sits in the grace-window replay queue and is replayed alongside the winning commit). This means AC-ORDER-3's dispatcher-delivered call count is NOT '2x the app-message count per cycle' as a naive read of 'replay' might suggest — the dispatcher's own rumor-id LRU silently collapses the replay's re-emission back down to exactly one handler call per cycle. Worth flagging for S5's behavior-docs pass since it's a real, load-bearing dedup interaction between two files that isn't obviously implied by either file's own comments in isolation. [Round 1] EpochResolver's onApplicationMessage callback has NO dedup of its own (unlike the dispatcher) — it genuinely fires twice per rollback cycle (once at the message's initial ingest, once during replay), confirmed empirically via a debug probe. The original AC-ORDER-3 assertion (`toHaveBeenCalled()`, no upper bound) did not pin this and would have silently accepted an extra spurious invocation — a real, mutation-confirmed tautology, closed in this round by asserting the exact `count * 2`.
